Wrong. One reason computers cannot replace a human programmer entirely is the halting problem. This is the problem of determining, from a description of an arbitrary computer program and an input, whether the program will finish running or continue to run forever. Alan Turing proved that a general algorithm to solve the halting problem for all possible program-input pairs cannot exist.

This means that a computer cannot identify whether or not a program will enter an infinite loop or not without a proof written specifically for that program. Any programmer who wrote a program that could generate such proofs would be writing exactly the algorithm Turing proved was impossible.

This means that for any program, a human must come up with the formal proof that it will even terminate, let alone that it will do what they want it to do. At some level, no matter how much code is automatically generated, software will always require human intervention.

So while I can't deny that there is some possibility we may create a hitherto inconceivable AI that can accomplish this task, the chance of us suddenly discovering how to do the impossible is at best a fantasy.

You're making two massive assumptions here: One, that humans can solve the halting problem, in the general case - consider the whole P != NP situation. We can't even definitively prove the order of complexity of some algorithms, let alone definitively prove whether an arbitrary algorithm halts. And two, that humans are noncomputable (and hence can do things that a Turing machine cannot do).

I would posit that humans ARE the solution to the halting problem. We are perfectly capable of creating formal proofs for many complex algorithms. While this is not the complete set of all algorithms, it is larger than those done by computers. And because each proof must be created for each algorithm as it is discovered, there is no advantage to even attempting to automate the process. You need to create the proof only once. After that, you need only test the program against the manually created specifications.

On some level, we will always need a human to translate a real-world need into a specification, then instruct a computer how to build the program to meet that specification. Tools may get better to where we hardly need to write code, but there will always be demand for intelligent abstract thinkers.
